strengths: Clear and valuable conceptual contribution: the paper carefully disentangles three previously conflated notions of Gaussian universality (performance, score, minimizer) and situates the work relative to a large body of RMT/AMP/CGMT/Lindeberg literature via a comprehensive comparison table (Table 1).

The quadratic universality result for smooth regularizers (Theorem 3.3/Proposition 3.1) is a clean, rigorously proved technical contribution that reduces general C^2 convex regularizers to an explicit quadratic surrogate depending only on local second-order structure.

The min-max/fixed-point characterization (Theorems 4.3/4.4) elegantly generalizes many known asymptotic formulas from the RMT/AMP/CGMT literatures (e.g., recovering Karoui et al. 2013, Bean et al. 2013, Donoho & Montanari 2016 as special cases), unifying disparate results under one framework.

Theorem 6.1 gives a sharp, interpretable if-and-only-if criterion for score universality (Gaussianity of x^Tμ* determines Gaussianity of the score), directly explaining when and why universality breaks down rather than just detecting breakdown empirically.

The subspace confinement result (Theorem 7.1, Corollary 7.2) yields a practically checkable geometric sufficient condition for score universality in signal-plus-noise models, connecting abstract theory to concrete model structure.

Empirical validation spans synthetic bimodal-feature models, an elastic-net interpolation study, and a real-data MNIST classification experiment (Appendix G), consistently showing that the proposed non-Gaussian theoretical predictions track empirical behavior much more closely than naive Gaussian-moment-matched surrogates or Gaussian score assumptions.

The paper is transparent about which components are proven versus conjectural/assumed, and provides an extensive appendix with detailed proofs for the rigorously established parts (concentration of θ-hat, quadratic universality, connections to prior RMT derivations for ridge regression).
weaknesses: The central technical engine of the paper, the 'Generalized CGMT for concentrated column designs' (Claim 4.1), is explicitly stated by the authors to be 'still only a conjecture,' yet essentially all headline results (Theorem 4.3, Theorem 4.4, and everything downstream including the score-universality theorem and subspace confinement corollary) depend on it. This significantly undercuts the soundness of claims phrased as proofs ('we show,' 'we prove') in the abstract and main text.

The second pillar underlying the fully explicit score-universality result, Assumption 4 ('minimizer universality'), is also an unproven standing assumption; the authors state a proof 'is under preparation' via Chatterjee's method, meaning Theorem 6.1 -- arguably the paper's most cited practical takeaway -- is not rigorously established either.

Assumption 2 requires C^2, strongly convex regularizers, explicitly excluding Lasso/L1 and other non-smooth penalties that are central to much of the high-dimensional statistics literature this paper aims to generalize, limiting the practical scope of the rigorous results.

The empirical validation, while illustrative, is relatively narrow in scale (small p,n toy examples, one real dataset with a simple binary MNIST merge) and does not include systematic ablations over dimension scaling, sample complexity, or computational cost/convergence behavior of solving the high-dimensional min-max/fixed-point system.

The gap between the paper's framing (definitive characterization of universality breakdown) and its actual epistemic status (a conjectural framework validated primarily by simulation) should be more prominently and consistently flagged in the abstract, introduction, and contributions list, since a reader skimming these sections could reasonably believe the core claims are unconditionally proven.

The presentation is dense, with substantial technical content deferred to a lengthy appendix; some readers may find it hard to assess exactly which theorems are unconditional versus contingent on Assumption 4/Claim 4.1 without careful cross-referencing.

strengths: The paper provides a valuable and precise taxonomy distinguishing performance universality, score universality, and minimizer universality — three notions that had been conflated or used inconsistently in prior literature — and uses this taxonomy to organize a large, carefully curated related-work table (Table 1) covering RMT, AMP, CGMT, and Lindeberg-based approaches.

The framework unifies and recovers several strands of the exact-asymptotics literature (e.g., Karoui et al. 2013, Bean et al. 2013, Donoho & Montanari 2016, Mai & Liao's LFMM equations) as special cases of a single fixed-point system (Theorem 4.4), which is a nontrivial synthesis effort documented explicitly in Appendix D and F.

Theorem 7.1 (covariance-adjusted subspace confinement) gives a clean, interpretable geometric result showing how anisotropic noise skews the direction of the asymptotic estimator mean away from the naive signal subspace, and directly explains the structural source of score non-Gaussianity.

The paper is empirically grounded with both controlled synthetic experiments (bimodal features, elastic loss) and a real-data example (MNIST), explicitly demonstrating cases where moment-matched Gaussian surrogates fail to predict both the score distribution and the generalization performance, which supports the paper's central qualitative claim.

The authors are transparent about the conjectural status of their central technical tool (Claim 4.1) and the minimizer-universality assumption (Assumption 4), clearly labeling downstream results as conditional rather than overclaiming full rigor.

Extensive proof appendix (25+ pages) with detailed derivations, stability lemmas, and an independent RMT-based consistency check (Appendix D.2) for the ridge regression case, lending some cross-validation to the fixed-point equations even where the general CGMT extension is unproven.
weaknesses: The paper's central technical device, the non-Gaussian extension of CGMT (Claim 4.1), is explicitly stated as a conjecture rather than a proven comparison principle; nearly all headline results (Theorem 4.3, Theorem 4.4, and consequently Theorem 3.3 and Corollary 5.1) are conditional on this unproven claim, which is a significant soundness gap for results labeled 'Theorem.'

A second load-bearing assumption, minimizer universality (Assumption 4), which underlies the main score-characterization result (Theorem 6.1), is also unproven within the paper; its justification is deferred to an unpublished, in-preparation manuscript (Louart, 2026), making an important part of the argument currently unverifiable by readers.

The chain of conditional derivations (conjecture ⇒ deterministic fixed point ⇒ assumption ⇒ score law) means the paper's rigor is considerably weaker than the theorem-heavy presentation suggests; the practical takeaway is closer to a well-motivated heuristic framework than a fully established theory, which should be reflected more starkly in how results are framed (e.g., via 'Conjecture' or 'Heuristic Claim' labeling rather than 'Theorem' with post-hoc caveats).

Numerical validation is somewhat limited in scale and diversity: the main synthetic experiment uses very small n=50, p=30, and the MNIST experiment is a single coarse binary grouping; broader validation (varying n/p ratios, more loss/regularizer combinations, quantitative error bars on how well theory tracks empirics as n grows) would strengthen confidence that the asymptotic predictions are accurate outside curated examples.

The presentation is very dense, with heavy notation and many interlocking assumptions/theorems distributed across a long appendix; a clearer high-level summary distinguishing which results are unconditional versus which depend on Claim 4.1/Assumption 4 (e.g., in a table) would substantially improve readability and help readers gauge the actual certainty of each claim.

The degree of genuine novelty relative to the already extensive prior literature summarized in Table 1 is somewhat incremental in places — the paper's main new contribution is the explicit conceptual disentanglement and a broader (though conjectural) unifying fixed-point system, rather than a fundamentally new proof technique or previously inaccessible regime.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely important and topical question—precisely characterizing when Gaussian universality holds or breaks down for high-dimensional convex ERM—and proposes a taxonomy (performance/score/minimizer universality) that usefully organizes a fragmented literature (Table 1 is a valuable synthesis).

The derivation connects and partially unifies CGMT, RMT, and AMP-style fixed-point equations, and the appendix shows consistency with classical RMT deterministic equivalents (Section D.2) and recovers prior LFMM equations (Mai & Liao) as a special case, lending some internal coherence to the framework.

Section 7's covariance-adjusted subspace confinement result gives an interpretable geometric explanation for why non-Gaussianity can survive in the score even under signal-plus-Gaussian-noise structure, which is a conceptually appealing contribution.

The paper includes both synthetic simulations (elastic-loss teacher-student model) and a real-data example (MNIST) illustrating cases where naive Gaussian-moment-matching surrogates fail to predict performance.
weaknesses: The central technical engine of the paper, the non-Gaussian CGMT extension (Claim 4.1), is explicitly presented as a conjecture ("we conjecture that..."), and essentially every downstream result of consequence (Theorem 4.3, and by extension Theorem 3.3, Corollary 5.1, Theorem 6.1, Theorem 7.1) is stated as being "conditional on Claim 4.1" or on further unproven stability hypotheses. This means the paper's main claims are not actually established; they are heuristic consequences of an unverified comparison principle, which is a serious soundness gap for a paper whose title promises a "characterization."

A second load-bearing assumption, minimizer universality (Assumption 4), is also unproved; the paper defers its justification to an unpublished/forthcoming preprint ("Louart, 2026... under preparation"), so a reader cannot verify or reproduce this key ingredient at submission time. Relying on a non-public companion proof for the main asymptotic score result undermines self-containment and reproducibility.

The paper's presentation blurs the line between rigorously proved statements and conjecture-conditioned claims (e.g., Theorem 4.3 is labeled a "Theorem" despite depending on an explicitly conjectural comparison principle), which risks overstating the rigor of the contribution to a reader who does not carefully track the conditioning throughout.

Numerical validation is thin relative to the scope of claims: the main synthetic experiment uses very small dimensions (p=30, n=50), and the MNIST experiment (Appendix G) is only briefly described with no details on preprocessing dimensionality, regularization scheme, or multiple trials/error bars; there is no systematic exploration of how tight the asymptotic predictions are as n,p grow or how sensitive results are to violations of the stated assumptions.

Assumption 2's smoothness/strong-convexity requirement excludes non-smooth regularizers such as Lasso, which several of the cited comparison works (e.g., Stojnic, Thrampoulidis et al.) do handle via CGMT; this narrows the claimed generality relative to prior art in a way not clearly flagged in the main comparison table's framing.

The Software and Data section is truncated/incomplete in the manuscript (ends mid-sentence with no repository link or code description), and the Impact Statement is a boilerplate non-statement that adds no discussion of limitations or ethical considerations specific to this work.

The overall contribution reads as an incremental, technically dense extension/synthesis of existing CGMT, RMT, and AMP machinery (as the paper's own Table 1 comparison suggests) rather than a fundamentally new methodological or conceptual advance, and the practical takeaways (e.g., that moment-matching Gaussian surrogates can fail) largely reconfirm points already made in cited prior work (Pesce et al., Mai & Liao, Hu & Lu).

strengths: The paper provides a clear conceptual contribution by explicitly disentangling three previously conflated notions of Gaussian universality (performance, score, minimizer universality), and situates the work carefully against a large body of prior literature via a detailed comparison table (Table 1).

The theoretical framework is broad: it recovers as special cases several known results (Dobriban & Wager ridge regression, Karoui et al./Bean et al. fixed-point equations, Mai & Liao's LFMM equations), which is a non-trivial consistency check and increases confidence in the correctness of the derivations despite their heuristic derivation route.

The paper gives an explicit, interpretable criterion for score (non-)universality: x^T*theta-hat is asymptotically Gaussian iff x^T*mu_* is Gaussian, and further localizes the source of non-Gaussianity to the structured component in signal-plus-noise models (Theorem 7.1), which is conceptually illuminating and actionable.

Numerical experiments (synthetic bimodal-feature teacher-student model and an MNIST-based classification task) directly illustrate the theoretical claims, showing concrete cases where moment-matched Gaussian surrogates fail to predict performance/score distributions while the theory succeeds.

The appendix includes a substantial and reasonably self-contained proof apparatus (concentration of the minimizer, quadratic universality of the regularizer, RMT consistency checks, and multiclass extension), which aids reproducibility of the theoretical claims.
weaknesses: The central technical engine of the paper (Claim 4.1, the extension of CGMT to non-Gaussian concentrated designs) is explicitly stated as a conjecture rather than a proven theorem; nearly all headline results (Theorems 4.3, 6.1, 7.1, Corollary 5.1) are conditional on this unproven comparison principle, which is a significant soundness limitation despite the honesty of the disclosure.

Assumption 4 (minimizer universality), which is needed for the score-level characterization in Section 6, is also unproven within the paper; the authors cite a companion paper 'under preparation' (Louart, 2026) as future justification, meaning a load-bearing assumption currently rests on an unpublished, unverifiable reference.

The empirical validation is fairly limited in scale and diversity: the main synthetic illustration uses small dimensions (p=30, n=50), and the single real-data experiment (binary MNIST subset) is relegated to the appendix with relatively brief description; broader real-world or larger-scale validation would strengthen confidence in the practical relevance of the theory.

The paper is dense with many stacked assumptions (Poincaré concentration, smoothness/strong convexity, weak-separability-type Assumption 3, saddle-point stability, uniform integrability) whose joint plausibility in realistic settings is not deeply discussed, making it hard for readers to assess when the theory's preconditions genuinely hold in practice.

Minor presentation issues remain, e.g., the 'Software and Data' section is truncated/incomplete in the manuscript, and some derivations (e.g., in Appendix C, Proposition C.2) rely on formal max-min interchanges 'assumed' to be valid without rigorous justification, compounding the conjectural nature of the framework.
